title: The Place of the Meek
english: Exalting the value of the reward. And they received such an image: let someone be an owner and let him trust a laborer, and let him say to him: 'If you take care of it as is necessary and work it as is fitting, a gift I give it to you; have it as an inheritance.' We say that he received the inheritance not from works, but from the grace of the one willing. 'There is an inheritance to those serving the Lord' (2 Tim 2:19).

And yet, in a little while, the sinner will no longer exist. This is said: 'Do not be envious of those committing adultery, nor be envious of those practicing lawlessness' (1 John 3:10). God fashioned a lover of good as a creature. To be a lover of good is not to desire the temporary and present things; for the temporary and present things belong even to sinners. Therefore, do not be envious of them, whether they prosper or whether they are healthy; for they do not remain always. And if [gap]... I do not speak of the essence, but the quality.

Regarding the 'temporary'; if you wish to take it readily, he who seems to no longer sin is not a sinner. And then he does not enact the things of sin. But 'the enjoyment of sin is temporary' (1 John 2:17), as Paul writes. The enjoyment of sin no longer exists. Therefore, we say to the many that he who seems to no longer sin is no longer a sinner; but according to the true word: sin neither was from the beginning nor shall be unto the age (1 John 2:17); for concerning the most supreme kind of it, this idolatry, it has been said: 'neither from the beginning nor unto the age.'

And if the most surpassing of evils had no beginning, such as to be unceasing, nor would it ever receive a manifest end, 'yet in a little while the sinner will not exist.' You also have in the ninth Psalm: 'Break the arm of the sinner and the wicked' (Ps 9:9). He did not say 'a sinner,' but 'the.' And if 'the arm of the sinner' is broken, it is much more than the inferior. 'And you will seek his place and will not find' (Ps 9:10).

Again, readily: for it is necessary to speak even the more popular explanations. The place of the sinner seems to be the place concerning the earth; for here lawlessness happens, here sins are completed. Therefore the earth will pass away along with the heaven. 'And you will seek his place and will not find' (Ps 9:10). Place is mainly called the position of each. And indeed, concerning Judas it is said that he passed by the place of service: 'from which Judas passed by' (Acts 12:4).

A position is a place of service, such as the position according to service; for when Paul says, 'first apostles, second prophets, third,' they are shallow because they are revealed only by their position. Likewise, in military ranks they say one has the place of a benefit-receiver or an assistant, and similarly in the churches.

The place of the sinner will not be found if he is no longer a sinner; his place was sin. 'But the meek shall inherit the earth' (Ps 37:11). Shortly, the sinner will neither be seen nor his place found, even if searched for; the place of the meek remains for ever; for it is eternal, it is immortal. And concerning the righteous it is said, 'his righteousness remains unto the age of ages.'

Therefore the meek, that is, those having gentleness, those perfecting themselves in lack of anger, shall inherit the earth; for the one without anger is gentle; for one should not say of others that he is gentle if he becomes angry at those whom it is necessary to be angry with. This kind of gentleness is more political and rhetorical. What does that mean? For the excellent man is without anger; and it is said in the falling verses, 'cease from anger and leave wrath' (Ps 37:8).

And they shall delight in abundance of peace. When does this abundance of peace occur? When the prayer of those saying, 'grace to you and peace be multiplied' is heard. He who is able to say, 'among those hating peace I was peaceful,' has an abundance of peace, and delights in this abundance of peace. It is possible to say that, having been relocated from this land, where wars and disturbances occur, they become in the land of the meek, where peace is lived out.

I have also said elsewhere regarding this, in matters of practical application, 'what virtue is needed?' and he says that when all are righteous, there is no need for courage. But he calls courage the more political kind, that which stands together in wars. When all are righteous, there is no need for courage; but when courage is present, there is a need for righteousness. And there, therefore, they delight in abundance of peace, when they are gentle. And the gentle man, as it was said to us, has a tranquil disposition toward anger. And from the one teaching and preparing for the imitation of himself, the greatness of the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Protection of the Wing and the Character of the Just
english: Observe virtue: 'Learn from me,' he says, 'for I am gentle and low in heart.' He did not say 'lowly' simply, but 'low in heart.' According to the disposition, I am gentle; according to the heart. He who possesses blindness is 'low in heart.' Since the evangelical word has been uttered, those saying that Jesus lacked mind, but had an irrational soul, must be rebuked. In all the writings, both new and old, the heart is said instead of the mind; for when it says, 'Listen to me, you who have lost your heart,' it means those who have lost the capacity for thought. And 'stony heart' is a stony intellect. If therefore he has a heart and this also has virtue—for he is gentle in heart and low—he has taken up a perfect man.

The sinner will watch the righteous man and gnash his teeth at him (Ps 35:16). This says that the sinner always wants to be an enemy of the righteous, and not only an enemy, but wants to be a murderer against him. And see how 'will watch' lies; primarily this watching means to observe how one might harm someone. What kind of person is armed? He who wants to shoot him with an arrow watches which part of him is naked, and where he sends the arrow. Since therefore the righteous is protected, he is not naked, but has put on 'the armor of God' (Eph 6:11) and 'has taken up the breastplate of faith' (Eph 6:14) and is entirely secured.

If, however, 'will watch' is instead of 'will keep'—for often verbs said after an intention mean the same, such as 'going' and 'descending'; the one descending goes down—if it is 'will keep,' then two things are meant, either that to watch has been said or to guard. If indeed the Savior says in the Gospel, 'Holy Father, keep them' (John 17:11), he says, 'protect them.' 'When I was with them, I kept them' (John 17:12), if it is of 'was guarding.' And those saying, 'You will preserve us from this generation' (Luke 21:36), say, 'you will protect.' It means, as I have said, to 'keep' is to 'watch/observe.' It is said, therefore, 'He will keep your head, and you his wing.' The saint watches the head of the serpent, so that having risen up the head of his evil, he might leave the whole thing dead. But the serpent is not able to keep the head of the man, but the wing, the extremities...

He preserves his powers that approach the earth. No serious wound or harm occurs upon the wing. For it has been said also in other places: 'The iniquity of my wing will surround me; then I was afraid in the evil day' (Ps 90:7). If the iniquity had kept my head, it would have clung to my head like that one, concerning whom it is written: 'His pain will turn back upon his head' (Prov 22:8). And again: 'I gave their ways into their heads' (Prov 19:3), instead of: 'into their mind.' And it is good also to say 'the righteous,' not simply 'righteous,' but the perfect righteous, the irreproachable; for it is said many times also concerning those progressing in name who are accused according to the perfect, such as: 'The wise do not depart from the mouth of the Lord' (Ps 119:105). No one of the wise becomes outside the word of the Lord, always working with the word. And it is said: 'Rebuke a wise man and he will love you' (Prov 9:8). Behold, a wise man.

The sinner borrows and does not repay, but the righteous shows mercy and gives. He not only returns what he borrowed, but also becomes a benefactor to others. By showing mercy, he gains. 'He who shows mercy to the poor lends to God' (Prov 19:17). The one borrowing from God is righteous, having gathered a multitude of works and of reasonable silver, and he benefits another; for the evil ones harm those who are with them, but the righteous ones benefit. And that the evil one is harmful is manifest. For it has been said in proverbs that the wise man benefits and improves: 'Rebuke a wise man and he will love you' (Prov 9:8). Being rebuked, he receives the rebukes well as to love the one rebuking him. But having loved the one rebuking him, he no longer works the things upon which the rebuke occurred. Just as 'he is a brother to the one who loathes himself' (Prov 27:11), the one doing evil. Therefore, the evil one harms himself above all.

The righteous, therefore, shows mercy and gives, and he is full of grace and simply participates in good things toward his neighbor. Those saying that, 'if a brother or sister are naked and lacking of the daily food' (Matt 25:35), that is: 'Go in peace, be satisfied,' but do not give to them the necessities, did not benefit them, since they do not 'show mercy and give.' And it is possible also to take it thus: the sinner, borrowing from God the common concepts given to him and the commandments, 'does not repay.'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Blessing and Cursing in Relation to Justice
english: Neither what he has nor what he received, nor the profit nor the interest. 'But the righteous' [Ps 112:5] God even more 'shows mercy and gives.' He who receives does not give back, but he himself even more 'shows mercy and gives.' And I say: then the mercy and the benevolence appear, if the receiver is ungrateful. 'He is kind even to the ungrateful and the evil,' [Matt 25:34] he gives. Those receiving are ungrateful—for by not giving back what is necessary to give back, they are found ungrateful and evil—but God is still kind even to these. Therefore the righteous even more shows mercy and provides.

The imitator, therefore, of God, 'who shows mercy to the poor and lends to God' [Ps 112:4], even if the one being lent to does not provide what he owes to provide, he is still merciful, he still provides. And take for me the parable of the Gospel concerning the talents: 'to each according to his own ability' [Matt 25:15] he gave the rational things belonging to him, not to each according to his nature, but according to the ability which he himself had prepared by choice. 'And to the one he gave five, to the other two, to the other one' [Matt 25:15]. 'The one having received five talents worked with them' [Matt 25:16] and doubled them. Having borrowed, he paid back. The one with two likewise. The one having received the one and having buried it in the earth, neither worked with it nor gave interest, he hid it in the earth [Matt 25:18].

When you see a man having the ability to do good or to be a philanthropist and not doing it, he has buried what he received into the earth, he has buried it into his own material choice. And being asked for it, when the time remained to 'gather' [Matt 25:19] to those who had received the rational silver, he says: 'See, you have the sponge' [Matt 25:24]. And he accused God, wanting to write his own slowness upon another: 'I knew,' [Matt 25:24] he says, 'I knew that you are a hard man, removing what you did not set, reaping where you did not sow; and having been afraid, you hid your silver in the earth' [Matt 25:22-23] and to no one did you give it. From which things he said, he had the rebuke and the condemnation: 'Man, wicked slave, you knew that I remove what I did not set' [Matt 25:26], if I remove not what is mine, I overstepped my own, not what was received; if 'I reap where I did not sow' [Matt 25:23]? In any case, they were taking mine, if you had given it on a table so that it might be multiplied. Therefore, even this was deprived. And the sinner, therefore, many times...

If one is rising up but does not pay back what he owes to pay back, his benefits will one day be taken away. He will no longer receive from the righteous, much more from one pitying and providing. 22 For those blessing him shall inherit the land. Those blessing the righteous. One must receive both kinds of returns: namely, the righteous man or God. He who does those things which God requires of him blesses God, so as to say: 'I will bless the Lord at all times' (Ps 112:1). And the righteous man is blessed: 'for the blessing of the Lord is upon the head of the righteous' (Ps 112:3), and: 'this one shall receive blessing from the Lord' (Ps 37:3). 'The land,' that land, concerning which it was said: 'and he will lift you up to inherit the land' (Ps 37:11).

22 But those cursing him shall be destroyed. Therefore the impious one curses the righteous by speaking about him, or toward those whom he speaks to: 'Woe to them, because they have departed from me; they are wretched, because they have done evils against me; I redeemed them, but they spoke lies against me.' 'I,' he says, 'redeemed them,' meaning he led them into the bath of regeneration, having freely granted the complete forgiveness of sins, having wiped out their lawlessness. But they speak lies against me, not doing those things for which they were called. And they had the forgiveness of sins; for not for this purpose did I redeem them, so that they might sin, but so that they might become outside of sin. If, therefore, after the ransoms and the means, someone does something absurd, he speaks lies by saying in a certain way: 'He did not benefit me,' he says lies against him.

23 The steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and he will desire his way (Ps 37:23). The man walks volitionally from the inferior to the superior, from the temporal to the eternal. And to him belongs the willing of the good, since it is 'not of him who runs nor of him who wills, but of the God who shows mercy' (Rom 9:16) to successfully complete the way. 'The steps of a man are directed by the Lord.' The steps are not given; for it is ours to will to walk from the bad to the good. Immediately, indeed, in the epistle of John, he writes: 'We know that we have passed from death to life' (1 Jn 5:13). 'We have passed,' not 'we were led.' God, directing the steps, did not force us into this by violence.
